prompt: By this lesson, what does a test environment consist of?

choices.text: The server the application is installed on while it is tested
choices.why: The machine is the first item, not the whole of it.

choices.text: Everything the application runs on and talks to
choices.why: Right: versions, settings, clock, data, mail and the browser too.

choices.text: The test cases, and the data each of them needs in order to run
choices.why: Cases and data are what you bring; the environment is what they run in.

choices.text: The copy of production that the client signs off before a release
choices.why: That describes staging, which is one environment among four.

prompt: Match each environment to what it is for.
hint: Each step is closer to the customers.

pairs.right: A developer writing code, minute by minute
A known build that testers install and reset
The release candidate, as close to production as possible
Real customers, real data, real e-mail

right_distractors: A copy of the code kept for audits

prompt: A release passes every case in staging. What decides how much that pass is worth?

choices.text: How many cases were run there
choices.why: Many cases in an environment unlike production still miss what production does differently.

choices.text: Whether the client watched the run
choices.why: The client sees a run; the machine underneath is what the pass describes.

choices.text: How closely staging resembles production
choices.why: Right: parity is what lets a staging result speak for production.

choices.text: How long the build has been installed on staging
choices.why: Age changes nothing; a difference from production does.

prompt: Why does a tester still run a short check in production after a release?
hint: Lesson 1 left one thing for that moment.

choices.text: Because production is the cheapest place to find defects
choices.why: A defect found there has already reached a customer.

choices.text: Some things exist only there, such as the real mail server
choices.why: Right: the real domain, mail server and card machine are nowhere else.

choices.text: Because the staging results do not count until they are repeated there
choices.why: Staging counts to the degree it resembles production; nothing is repeated wholesale.

choices.text: To run the full regression suite on real customer data
choices.why: Production is not a test environment; a smoke check is short on purpose.

prompt: Which of these are part of boxoffice's environment? Choose all that apply.
hint: Would changing it change what you are testing?

choices.text: The value of BOXOFFICE_NOW it was started with
choices.why: Yes: it moves the application's clock.

choices.text: The time zone of the machine it runs on
choices.why: Yes, and defect 9 lives there.

choices.text: The version of Python
choices.why: Yes: it runs the program.

choices.text: The requirement R4
choices.why: A requirement is what you test against, the same in every environment.

choices.text: The title of the defect report
choices.why: The report describes the testing; nothing runs on it.

prompt: Read literally, what does "it works on my machine" tell a tester?

choices.text: That the report was wrong and can be closed
choices.why: Rui's result was true, and so was the tester's.

choices.text: Something differs between the two machines
choices.why: Right: that difference is part of the defect, and the job is to find it.

choices.text: That the tester used the wrong build
choices.why: Possible, and one of many differences; the phrase does not say which.

choices.text: That the developer's machine is the reference everybody should copy
choices.why: The customers use production, not the developer's laptop.

prompt: Order the steps Ana took to turn "works on my machine" into a defect anybody can repeat.
items: Pin the clock to the moment of the report with BOXOFFICE_NOW
Reproduce the developer's result with TZ=America/Sao_Paulo
Change only the zone to UTC and see the result flip
Try moments either side of the edge to find when it closes
trap: Searching the code first skips the two runs that prove where the difference is.

prompt: Why did Ana start boxoffice with BOXOFFICE_NOW set, instead of testing at 17:30 by the real clock?
hint: She wanted to change one thing.

choices.text: So only the zone differed between the two runs
choices.why: Right: hold everything still but one setting, and the flip names the cause.

choices.text: Because the defect cannot happen on the real clock
choices.why: It happens on the real clock every afternoon; pinning only makes it repeatable.

choices.text: Because BOXOFFICE_NOW also sets the machine's time zone
choices.why: It moves only the application's clock; TZ sets the zone.

choices.text: To make the confirmation links come out the same on every run
choices.why: That is BOXOFFICE_SEED, and it plays no part in this defect.

prompt: On Linux and macOS, a program reads the time zone from the environment variable `___`.
On a machine set to UTC, how many hours before the 19:00 cut-off does booking for The Seagull close, in São Paulo time?
hint: The 15:59 and 16:01 runs bracket the edge.

prompt: Which sentence explains defect 9 in a way that stays true however Rui fixes it?

choices.text: Line 214 uses the wrong timedelta
choices.why: A guess at code: it names a line the tester never read and may be wrong.

choices.text: The server is broken and has to be set back to São Paulo time
choices.why: That changes the environment to hide the defect; the program stays wrong.

choices.text: It compares São Paulo times with the machine's own clock
choices.why: Right: observed in two runs, and true whatever the fix turns out to be.

choices.text: Booking closes early on some days and on others it does not
choices.why: True of the symptom, but it hides the one setting that decides it.

prompt: Match each reading to where it comes from.
hint: One of them is not in the terminal.

prompt: During a capture, `date` printed 04:11 while boxoffice believed it was 14:00. What does that tell you?

choices.text: The machine's clock was wrong and should be corrected first
choices.why: The machine's clock was the real time; nothing needs correcting.

choices.text: The capture was made in another time zone than the one printed
choices.why: The `-03` on the same line is the zone it ran in.

choices.text: BOXOFFICE_NOW moved the application's clock and nothing else
choices.why: Right: so a report must say how the program was started.

choices.text: boxoffice ignores BOXOFFICE_NOW on Linux
choices.why: It read it: it believed 14:00, which is the value it was given.

prompt: Rui opens your report of defect 9 and gets an order. Which missing line most likely caused that?
hint: He started it the ordinary way.

choices.text: The browser in use and the exact version it reported
choices.why: Defect 9 shows up from curl too; no browser is involved.

choices.text: How it was started: TZ and BOXOFFICE_NOW
choices.why: Right: without it he runs on São Paulo time, and books.

choices.text: The version of Python the reporter had installed
choices.why: Both Python versions in this story run boxoffice the same way.

choices.text: The name and release of the operating system
choices.why: Ubuntu on both machines; the zone is what differed.

prompt: Why should the readings be pasted from the commands rather than typed?

choices.text: Pasting is faster than typing
choices.why: Speed is a bonus; the reason is accuracy.

choices.text: Tracking tools refuse typed version numbers
choices.why: No tool can tell typed from pasted text.

choices.text: From memory, 1.1 quietly becomes 1.0
choices.why: Right: a version typed from memory names a build you were not running, and the report describes a defect it never had.

choices.text: The commands print extra details nobody would think of typing
choices.why: They print one short line each; the point is that the line is right.

prompt: A price reads R$ 1.234,50 on staging and R$ 1,234.50 in production, from the same build. Where does a tester look first?

choices.text: At the code that formats money, for a recent change
choices.why: The build is the same in both places, so the code cannot be what differs.

choices.text: At the two machines' locale settings
choices.why: Right: same code, different result, so the difference is in the environment.

choices.text: At the browser each customer uses
choices.why: The two screens come from two servers; the browsers did not choose the separator.

choices.text: At the test data, which may hold a different price
choices.why: The amount is the same; only the separators moved.

prompt: Why did most test runs pass on both machines although defect 9 was there all along?
hint: When does a UTC machine close The Seagull?

choices.text: The defect appears only in the 1.1 release
choices.why: The comparison is in the booking rule, which 1.1 did not touch.

choices.text: Testers always book Hamlet, which is not affected
choices.why: Hamlet closes three hours early on UTC too, on its own day.

choices.text: Both accept every booking before 16:00
choices.why: Right: the defect only shows in the three hours before the real cut-off.

choices.text: curl hides the message that the browser would have shown
choices.why: curl showed the closed message in the UTC run.

prompt: The word for how closely staging resembles production is ___.
A colleague on Windows wants to reproduce the UTC run. What does this lesson tell them?
hint: The zone lives somewhere else there.

choices.text: Type the same TZ=UTC command line in PowerShell
choices.why: That syntax is a Unix shell's; PowerShell does not read it.

choices.text: Set the computer's own time zone to UTC, then start it
choices.why: Right, with BOXOFFICE_NOW set, and the zone set back afterwards. Not run for this course.

choices.text: The defect cannot happen on Windows
choices.why: It depends on the machine's zone, which Windows has like any system.

choices.text: Use BOXOFFICE_NOW alone, with a UTC offset in the value
choices.why: The value moves the instant; the comparison still uses the machine's zone.
